source.title: A Hitchhiker's Guide to Scaling Law Estimation
source.authors: Leshem Choshen; Yang Zhang; Jacob Andreas

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices through Figure 9; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates how well fitted scaling laws predict held-out losses and finds that accuracy depends on family, training checkpoints, and model selection; it also identifies substantial variation among fitted family parameters.
record.gate_note: The paper fits the Hoffmann et al. functional form to published model-family data and evaluates loss predictions. Downstream evaluations are collected but not analyzed as results here. Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is not tested. Results cited from other studies, including initialization variance and data-ablation effects, are not recorded as rows. Figure 2 and other plots contain additional values not individually transcribed where the text does not assign exact values to a condition.
record.test_reason: The study independently evaluates held-out loss extrapolation and shows how prediction reliability and fitted parameters depend on model family, training-model selection, and checkpoint coverage. Its clearest tests concern V2 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's conclusion is substantially accurate. The authors recommend intermediate checkpoints excluding the earliest training, generally favor models nearer the target size, and find that additional smaller models can improve robustness. Borrowed scaling coefficients sometimes permit accurate prediction from one target-family run. Seed variability is their interpretation of instability, rather than a newly controlled seed experiment.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the Hoffmann et al. functional form and held-out loss prediction, but performs a meta-analysis of previously published families rather than a new controlled scaling sweep. It fits with curve_fit and square loss, targets the 30%-maximal-token family, and reports mean absolute relative error; some analyses use intermediate checkpoints and cross-family parameter borrowing.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction accuracy changes with the model family and selected training models, their proximity to the target size, number of models, checkpoint coverage, exclusion of the first 10B tokens, and fit loss (square versus Huber, with overall trends reported as similar).

fits_no_version.finding: Unfitted best-model baselines average 18% absolute relative error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extrapolation can improve loss estimates relative to simply using the best observed training-model loss.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267, 2025
record.problems: The analysis aggregates heterogeneous published families and training conditions; the paper notes substantial prediction variability and that a single model can affect estimates. Many plotted results are not accompanied by exact values in the text. The authors also state that their ARE metric does not distinguish over- from under-estimation and that incomparable family scales prevented an informative aggregate analysis of compute-optimal preliminary experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No further separately quantified result rows were left out. Additional Figure 2, Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 6, Figure 8, and Figure 9 plot condition-specific errors or predictions without all corresponding values being stated in the text; these were not transcribed individually. Cited results and collected-but-not-analyzed downstream evaluations were excluded.

untested.parts: The study assumes the additive power-law form and evaluates predictions; it does not separately establish bottleneck-controlled power-law loss scaling over several orders of magnitude.
Orders-of-magnitude extrapolation is not established by the sevenfold OLMO example, the smaller OPT scale factors, or same-model partial-training predictions.
No test of stable compute-optimal parameter and token allocation powers.
No controlled fixed-parameter comparison quantifying the loss effects of depth, width, or architecture.
Repeated-data families appear in coefficient comparisons, but the paper does not establish the power-law form in those regimes or in other modalities, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream evaluations are collected but not analyzed for scaling predictability.
Parameter-counting conventions, compute-optimal splits, and systematic departures from a single power law are not tested. Learning-rate schedule explanations remain hypotheses.

missing.what: Cross-validation fails to identify harmful training models: removing the model selected by the proposed diagnostic produces the worst target ARE in 58% of cases. This supplies additional evidence of model-selection sensitivity.
The text explicitly reports reliable prediction of a 34-fold larger Pythia model with suitable training-model selection, complementing the failure of the smallest Pythia models.

record.verdict_notes: Verdicts use only the supplied text. Successful fitting and family-specific exponents do not by themselves limit V1. The supplied text also contains an identifier inconsistency: its reference list assigns arXiv:2410.11840 to SLOTH, although its header assigns it to this study; bibliographic identity should be checked separately.

versions.untested_parts: Does not independently compare alternative functional forms or establish power-law behavior for parameters, tokens, and compute separately over specified orders of magnitude.
Does not provide a uniform test of extrapolation across every family or a systematic test of departures from a power law at very large scales.
No test of the loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation as a function of a fixed compute budget.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
No tests in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream evaluations are included in the dataset, but the paper's experiments reported here focus on held-out loss.
Does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, compute-optimal allocation fits, or alternative functional forms; it notes that learning-rate schedules may need explicit treatment.

rows.subject: scaled model families (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: 485 pretrained models across more than 40 scaled families
rows.operation_detail: Fit the Hoffmann et al. scaling-law form to family training models and evaluate loss predictions on held-out target models.
rows.measure: Mean absolute relative error of predicted held-out loss
rows.value: The paper reports that scaling-law estimation is noisy; in small model families error does not reliably decrease with additional computation.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result across the paper's scaling-law estimation experiments.
rows.check: Prediction variability does not directly establish or refute V1's power-law form. For V7, the reported dependence on model selection is observed. The 485 models describe the collected dataset, not necessarily every experiment. Targets are largest-parameter models trained on at least 30% of the maximum token count.

rows.subject: OLMO family
rows.operation_detail: Fix parameter-scaling parameters to values reported by Muennighoff et al. and estimate the remaining parameters using one model in the new family.
rows.measure: Absolute relative error in predicting target loss
rows.note: The text describes predicting a 7B model from a collection of 1B model checkpoints and reports that OLMO is an example where a single run in the new family suffices.
rows.check: The less-than-1% error is correct, but 1B to 7B does not test extrapolation over orders of magnitude. This uses borrowed parameter-scaling coefficients plus target-family checkpoints. The result alone does not demonstrate V7 dependence. Locator is Section 5, rather than Section 5.1.

rows.measure: Absolute relative error in predicted loss
rows.note: The paper reports this as an example of larger errors when predicting across model families.
rows.check: The 37% error shows poor extrapolation under borrowed parameter-scaling coefficients, rather than an unrestricted within-family fit. The source-size dependence is observed for V7. Section 5 reports these numbers.

source_check.correct: OPT loss-prediction ARE is 37% for the stated 8.7B-to-175B extrapolation. A and α are fixed to values from Muennighoff et al.; remaining parameters are estimated within the target family. V2: partial under this restricted protocol. V7: cannot_determine from this error alone.

rows.subject: Pythia

rows.subject: OPT, GPT-3, and Pythia families
rows.operation_detail: Compare scaling-law fits using training checkpoints across the trajectory with fits based only on end-of-training checkpoints.

conditions.value: intermediate checkpoints versus end of training

rows.measure: Absolute relative error in final-loss prediction
rows.value: Including full training curves can predict losses well; relying only on end-of-training data produces significantly worse performance across the board. After discarding the first approximately 10% of checkpoints, final loss can often be predicted accurately.
rows.note: The text states the trend for the plotted families; the plots separately show OPT, GPT-3, and Pythia.
rows.check: Split successful trajectory-based predictions from poorer end-only fits. Checkpoint dependence is observed for V7. The first approximately 10% exclusion is a Figure 4 qualification, not a uniform condition for every comparison. Figure 4's caption and the prose disagree about the left/right orientation.

source_check.correct: Intermediate checkpoints generally improve prediction over end-only fits. Figure 4 qualifies accurate predictions by excluding approximately the first 10% of checkpoints. V2: partial across conditions. V7: cannot_determine for exponents or allocation from ARE alone.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state does not distinguish prediction reliability from V7's exponent/allocation claim.

rows.check: The numerical comparison is supported, but 4–10% is a range reported jointly for examples including OPT and Pythia, not an exact OPT estimate. Checkpoint-selection dependence is observed for V7.

rows.subject: scaled model families (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compare fitted scaling-law parameter estimates across model families.

conditions.value: E, A, α, B, and β

rows.measure: Variation and relationships among fitted parameters
rows.value: The five parameters often differ dramatically across families; three principal components explain 99.49% of their variance, and the size- and token-related parameter pairs show clear linear relationships. T5-Pile and four families trained with multiple passes over a single training set are noted as exceptions.
rows.note: This is evidence that fitted scaling behavior varies across families, alongside regularities among fitted parameters.
rows.check: Variation in fitted coefficients supports setup dependence, not a limitation of V1: V1 does not require identical exponents across families. Separate coefficient variation from the PCA result. The repeated-data exceptions concern the B–β relationship, not demonstrated failure of the power-law form.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 5 and 9; Figure 3; Section 3.1 for dataset coverage

rows.subject: target models within the same parameter-count family (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Predict a model's final loss from partially trained checkpoints of the same parameter-count family, fitting the token-scaling term.

conditions.value: up to 30% of the full training run

rows.value: Reliable estimates may require up to 30% of the full training run; the approach is described as informative under suitable computational constraints.
rows.note: The paper presents this as an alternative to fitting from many smaller models.
rows.check: Dependence on training progress is supported. Predicting final loss after up to 30% of the same run does not establish V2's orders-of-magnitude extrapolation.

source_check.correct: Reliable token-axis extrapolation from a partially trained target model may require up to 30% of its full training run. V7: cannot_determine; this result reports prediction reliability rather than changes in fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation.
source_check.problem: Training-progress requirements do not directly establish the effect specified by V7.

rows.subject: scaled model families (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compare simple best-training-model baselines with target losses.

conditions.value: Best performance among training models or most-trained model

rows.measure: Absolute relative error in target-loss estimation
rows.baseline: Simple baselines without fitting a scaling law
rows.value: Baselines have more than 15% error even with the full family, are mostly above 10%, almost never below 5%, and average 18% ARE.
rows.note: These are comparison baselines, not fitted-law results.
rows.check: These are unfitted comparison baselines, not scaling-law predictions. Their errors cannot be assigned a state for V2 or V7. The prose's more-than-15% statement should not be treated as universal because it also reports values below that threshold.

rows.subject: OPT, Pythia, and Pythia deduped V0 families
rows.operation_detail: Repeat the scaling-law estimation analyses using Huber loss rather than square loss.
rows.value: Overall results and trends are similar to the main analysis.
rows.note: The appendix says the repeated analyses show the same trends; Figure 9 presents selected families.
rows.check: The square-to-Huber change retains the main trends, so dependence on this particular fitting choice is absent at the reported qualitative level. Figure 9 shows GPT-3, Pythia, GPT-2, and Llama, not the family list in the row. Preserve the supplied δ notation as ambiguous rather than silently correcting it.

source_check.correct: Appendix E reports similar overall results under Huber loss. Figure 9 shows GPT-3, Pythia, GPT-2 and Llama. V7: cannot_determine because qualitative prediction-error trends do not establish unchanged fitted exponents or allocation.
